title: Bildad: God Does Not Twist Justice
sum: Bildad, the second friend, answers Job with one firm principle: God does not twist justice (8:3). If Job's children died, they must have sinned. If Job is pure, he should seek God, and God will restore him so fully that his old life will look small (8:4–7). Bildad's authority is tradition: ask the generations before, whose wisdom is longer than one short life (8:8–10).

He then offers proverbs from that tradition. Papyrus without water withers before any other plant; the godless lean on a spider's house; a lush plant torn from its place is forgotten even by its place (8:11–19). He ends with a promise and a warning: God will not reject the wholehearted, and he will fill Job's mouth with laughter, while the tent of the wicked disappears (8:20–22).
readings: Read as sound teaching

Bildad states what much of the Bible teaches: God is just, sin destroys, and those who seek God are restored (Psalm 1; Psalm 37; Deuteronomy 30:1–10). His tone is less gentle than Eliphaz's, but he gives Job a real way forward: seek God, and your end will be greater than your beginning. On a first reading many hear him as a pastor offering hope.
Read with the prologue

The reader knows what Bildad does not. Job's children did not die for their sins (1:5; 1:18–19), and Job is exactly the wholehearted man Bildad says God will not reject (1:1; 8:20). Bildad's principle, applied without knowing the facts, turns into an accusation. His promise even comes true (42:12), but after God has said the friends spoke wrongly about him (42:7).

views.H: Readers who take Job as history see Bildad as a real sage of the East, whose speech reflects the wisdom of his time. His appeal to the fathers shows a world where truth was handed down by elders. The Talmud debates when Job lived, but treats the friends' words as real speeches to be weighed (Bava Batra 15b–16b).
views.C: Critical scholars read Bildad's speech as a skilled poem in which the friend speaks for traditional wisdom. Verses 11–19 may quote or imitate proverbs from the schools. Many note how each friend has a characteristic authority: Eliphaz a vision, Bildad tradition, Zophar God's hidden wisdom. The poet lets each speak strongly before the book judges them (42:7).
views.W: Bildad's argument has close parallels in the Babylonian Theodicy, a dialogue (perhaps 1000 BC) in which a sufferer complains and a friend replies that the gods' ways are just, the wicked prosper only briefly, and the pious will be rewarded. Like Bildad, the friend appeals to old wisdom and to images from nature. Unlike Job, the Babylonian sufferer ends by asking the gods for mercy, and the friend never meets a divine verdict.
views.J: Maimonides reads each friend as a school of thought on providence. Bildad stands for the view that suffering will be repaid by greater reward, so that Job's 'later years will grow very large' (8:7; Guide 3.23). Rashi reads 8:4 as Bildad saying the children were punished for their own sins. The rabbis praise the friends for coming to comfort, while blaming their words (Bava Batra 16b).
views.X: Christian preachers, from Gregory the Great to Calvin, have used Bildad as a warning against applying true doctrine without love or knowledge of the facts. Jesus rejects the reasoning of 8:4 when he says that those killed by Pilate or the tower of Siloam were not worse sinners than others (Luke 13:1–5), and that the man born blind was not punished for sin (John 9:1–3).

deep.b:
It is easy to dismiss the friends, since God says at the end that they did not speak rightly about him (42:7). But Bildad says nothing that cannot be found elsewhere in the Bible. God does not twist justice (Genesis 18:25; Deuteronomy 32:4). Sin brings its own ruin (Proverbs 5:22). Those who seek God are restored (Deuteronomy 30:1–10; Hosea 6:1). Life is short and we should learn from those before us (Psalm 90; Deuteronomy 32:7).

The problem is not his principles but their use. Bildad starts from a rule and reasons backward to Job's case: if God is just and Job suffers, Job must have sinned. Job starts from his own case and reasons forward to the rule: if I am innocent and I suffer, the rule as you state it is not true. The book does not settle the debate by declaring a winner in argument. It shows a God who is greater than both of their pictures (38–41), and who still says Job spoke rightly (42:7).

deep.title: Claude's theory: Bildad's three houses
deep.b: Bildad keeps returning to the word 'house': the spider's house (8:14), the house a man leans on that will not stand (8:15), the 'house of stones' the plant looks out on (8:17), and finally the tent of the wicked (8:22). I suspect this is aimed, consciously or not, at the house that fell on Job's children (1:19). Bildad's proverbs about fragile houses would land on Job as a comment on his own collapsed house. This is my own reading; commentators note the repetition of 'house' in 8:14–17 (Clines) but I have not seen the link to 1:19 drawn in this way.

settings.to: Job, sitting in the ashes (2:8), with Eliphaz and Zophar listening
settings.when: after Job's reply to Eliphaz (6–7), in which Job called his friends a dry stream and turned to complain to God
settings.why: to defend God's justice against Job's complaint, to explain the children's death as punishment, and to urge Job to seek God so that he can be restored. Bildad means it as both rebuke and hope.
settings.readers: For the book's first readers, likely Israelites after the exile, Bildad's words were familiar: the prophets and Deuteronomy had taught that disaster came from sin and that seeking God would bring restoration. Many believed it, and it explained the exile. The book lets Bildad state that faith at its best, and then asks its readers whether it fits every case, especially the righteous who suffer.
views: The friend as pastor
Some readers (Andersen) hear Bildad as sincerely offering Job hope, if bluntly.
The friend as prosecutor
Others (Clines, Newsom) hear the conditional sentences as accusations: Bildad's principle requires Job and his children to be guilty.

title: How Can Anyone Win a Case Against God?
sum: Job answers not Bildad but the question behind him: how can a mortal be in the right with God (9:2)? He turns it into a question of law. To win a case against God one would have to answer him, but God is the Creator who moves mountains, shakes the earth, commands the sun, tramples the Sea and made the stars (9:5–10). He passes by unseen, snatches with no one to stop him, and even the monsters of chaos bow to him (9:11–13).

So even an innocent man could not reply; he could only beg (9:14–21). Job dares to say that God destroys the wholehearted and the wicked alike, and laughs at the innocent (9:22–24). His days are flying away (9:25–26). No washing can make him clean in God's eyes (9:30–31). God is not a human he can meet in court, and Job wishes for someone to stand between them and judge the case (9:32–33). If only God would lift his rod, Job could speak without fear (9:34–35).
readings: Read as a lawsuit

Chapter 9 introduces the legal language that runs through the rest of the book: case, answer, summon, judge, guilty, innocent, umpire. Job is not asking how to be forgiven but how to get a fair hearing. The problem is structural: God is the opponent, the judge and the power, and there is no court above him.
Read as faith in crisis

Job never doubts that God exists or that he is all-powerful. What he cannot see is God's justice. His bold claims (9:22–24) are the words of a believer who still addresses God and still wants to be found right by him. Many readers find in this chapter the honest language of faith under pressure, like the lament psalms (Psalm 44; Psalm 88).
Read toward the end of the book

Job's complaints set up what follows. He says God crushes him 'in a windstorm' (9:17); God will speak from the windstorm (38:1). He says no one could answer God's questions (9:3); God will ask many (38–41). He wishes for someone to judge between them (9:33); his hope will grow into a witness in heaven (16:19) and a redeemer (19:25).

views.H: Traditional readers take Job's words as the real speech of a righteous man in agony. They note that God later says Job spoke rightly (42:7), but also that God rebukes him for 'darkening counsel' (38:2). Many conclude that Job's faith was sound and his words, in parts, rash.
views.C: Critical scholars see in chapter 9 the poet's boldest move: turning the friends' hymns into protest and the language of the law court into a way to speak about God. Many date the book to the 500s or 400s BC and read Job's questions as a challenge to the theology of Deuteronomy and the friends. The 'umpire' shows the poet's legal imagination.
views.W: Mesopotamian sufferers also complain of hidden divine ways. In 'I Will Praise the Lord of Wisdom' (Ludlul), the sufferer says he cannot know what pleases the gods. In the Babylonian Theodicy the sufferer asks why the gods favor the wicked. But no ancient text imagines a human taking his god to court with an umpire between them. Job's lawsuit is new.
views.J: The Talmud reads 9:17 as Job's complaint that God confused Iyyov (Job) with oyev (enemy), and 9:24 as Rava's charge that Job 'tried to turn the bowl upside down', denying justice, while Abaye answered that Job spoke of the Accuser (Bava Batra 16a). Rashi reads the umpire as the arbiter Job lacks before God. Jewish readers often hold that Job spoke in pain and was not punished for it.
views.X: Christian readers have heard in 9:33 a longing that Christ fulfills: one mediator between God and humans, himself human (1 Timothy 2:5). Gregory the Great and Thomas Aquinas both read the verse this way, and the KJV's 'daysman' became a name for Christ in hymns. Others, while seeing the echo, insist that Job himself states only his lack.

deep.b:
The figure Job longs for in 9:33, the mokhiach, is someone who 'sets things right' between two parties, an umpire or arbiter in a dispute (Genesis 31:37; Isaiah 2:4). The picture of laying a hand 'on each of us' may show the authority of a judge over both parties or the gesture of a go-between joining them. The Plain reads the line as a wish, with the Greek and Syriac; the received Hebrew says flatly that there is none (see the variant).

The image opens a line of hope that grows through Job's speeches. Here, a judge who is not there (9:33). Then a witness in heaven who will plead for a man with God (16:19–21). Then a redeemer (go'el) who will stand up on the dust at the last (19:25–27). Elihu speaks of an angel who intercedes for a man (33:23–24). Scholars debate whether these are one figure, or God himself (as God against God), or a hope Job reaches for without knowing who could fill it.

Christian readers saw the answer in Christ, the one mediator (1 Timothy 2:5; Hebrews 9:15). Jewish readers have often seen in it the hope for a heavenly advocate, or simply Job's protest at the unequal trial. All agree on Job's situation: he has no one.

The Greek. The Old Greek of Job is about a sixth shorter than the Hebrew, and Origen filled its gaps from Theodotion's version, marking the added lines with an asterisk. In chapters 8–14 the Greek covers almost every line; the large gaps come later in the book. One line here may be such a filler: Ziegler's Göttingen edition marks 9:3b with an asterisk, while Pietersma and Gentry argue it is original Old Greek. The Greek readings quoted on these pages are from Rahlfs' edition, checked directly for this site; Rahlfs does not print the asterisks, and Ziegler's edition was not checked for other marked lines.

Qumran. Two Hebrew fragments from Cave 4 cover parts of these chapters: 4QJob-b (8:15–17; 9:27; 13:4; 14:4–6) and 4QpaleoJob-c, written in the old Hebrew script (13:18–27; 14:13–18). As presented in a translation based on their official editions, they agree in meaning with the received Hebrew; one presentation shows the two halves of 14:15 in reverse order, which does not change the sense. They were seen for this site only through that translation, not the editions themselves. The Aramaic Job scroll from Cave 11 (11QtgJob) begins at 17:14, so it does not cover these chapters.

Aramaic and Latin. The later rabbinic Targum of Job, checked on Sefaria for 9:33 and 13:15, follows the received Hebrew at 9:33 and the reading tradition at 13:15. The Latin Vulgate readings are quoted from the standard edition, not checked line by line. The Syriac Peshitta was not checked; where it is cited, the report comes from the commentaries.

Job's hymn in 9:5–10 uses the same pictures as Israel's praise of the Creator: mountains moved, earth shaken on its pillars, the sun commanded, the heavens spread out, the Sea trampled, the stars made (Psalm 104; Amos 5:8; Isaiah 40:22–26). In praise, these acts mean that the God who is for us can do anything. In Job's mouth they mean that the God who is against him cannot be resisted. The same verse (9:10 = 5:9) proves both points. God's own speeches (38–41) will return to the same creation, the sea, the stars and the monsters, with a third meaning that Job does not yet imagine.

settings.what: Job's reply to Bildad: the impossible trial
settings.to: Bildad and the other two friends at first (9:2–24), then, more and more, God himself (9:28, 'you will not clear me'; 9:31)
settings.when: right after Bildad's speech, which told Job to seek God and be restored
settings.why: to show that Bildad's advice is impossible: Job cannot plead his case before a God who is both opponent and judge, and who seems to destroy the innocent with the guilty. Job speaks to expose the problem and to voice his longing for a fair hearing.
settings.readers: For the book's first readers, likely Israelites who had lived through or remembered the destruction of Jerusalem and exile, Job's words gave voice to a question the prophets also asked (Habakkuk 1:2–4; Lamentations 3): what if the suffering seems beyond any sin? The book allowed them to say this to God, in the form of a lawsuit, without leaving faith.

traditions.q: Job wishes for someone to stand between him and God (9:33), and Christians hear Christ, 'one mediator between God and humans' (1 Timothy 2:5). Does that one mediator rule out asking Mary and the saints to pray for us?
views: Catholic

Yes. Christ is the one mediator, and Mary and the saints share in his mediation in a subordinate way that 'neither takes away from nor adds anything to' his (Lumen Gentium 60–62; Catechism 969–970, 2683). Asking their prayers is like asking a fellow believer to pray.
Orthodox

Yes. The Theotokos and the saints are alive in Christ and pray for the church, and the faithful ask their intercession constantly in the liturgy, as the Seventh Ecumenical Council (Nicaea II, 787) affirmed.
Lutheran

No invocation. The saints may be remembered and honored as examples of faith, but Scripture does not teach calling on them for help, since it sets before us Christ alone as Mediator and Intercessor (Augsburg Confession 21, citing 1 Timothy 2:5).
Reformed
No. Christ alone is mediator in all his offices, and prayer is made to God through him alone; calling on saints or angels is rejected (Westminster Confession 8; 21.2; Second Helvetic Confession 5).
Baptist
No. Believers pray to God through Christ alone; the saints in heaven are not asked to intercede. Christians may and should pray for one another on earth (James 5:16).

title: Your Hands Made Me
sum: Job turns from the friends to God and speaks out of bitterness (10:1). He asks God not to condemn him without telling him the charge (10:2). Does God enjoy crushing his own handiwork while smiling on the wicked? Does he see like a human, with a short life, that he must hunt for Job's sin when he knows Job is not guilty (10:3–7)?

Then comes one of the most tender passages in the book: God's hands formed Job like clay, poured him like milk and set him like cheese, clothed him with skin and wove him with bones, gave him life and loyal love (10:8–12). But Job fears it was all a plan to watch and punish him (10:13–17). He returns to the wish of chapter 3: why was he born? Let God leave him alone for a little, before he goes to the land of darkness from which no one returns (10:18–22).
readings: Read as a prayer

Chapter 10 is a prayer, though a bitter one. Job speaks directly to God, asks him questions, reminds him of his own work, and asks for relief. It follows the pattern of the lament psalms: complaint, appeal to God's past care, a plea. Its honesty is part of its faith: Job still believes God is the one who can answer.
Read as an argument

Job builds a careful case. If God sees everything (10:4), he does not need to search for Job's sin (10:6). If God made Job with care (10:8–12), destroying him makes no sense (10:3; 10:9). Either God's care was a trap (10:13), or God is acting against his own nature. The chapter leaves that dilemma open.

views.H: Traditional readers see in 10:8–12 a beautiful confession of God as Creator of each person, taken up in Psalm 139. Many hold that Job's charge in 10:13 is the kind of rash speech God later corrects (38:2), while his trust in God's past care is sound.
views.C: Critical scholars read chapter 10 as a parody of the hymn of creation and of the 'trust' psalms. Job takes the language of God's care and asks what it means if that care ends in destruction. Many compare Psalm 139, which may draw on similar traditions, and Psalm 8, which Job has already parodied (7:17–18).
views.W: Egyptian and Mesopotamian texts also picture gods forming humans: the Egyptian potter-god Khnum shapes the child on his wheel, and the Mesopotamian goddess Mami (Nintu) mixes clay with divine blood in Atrahasis. Job's picture of God personally shaping him in the womb fits this world, but Job's God is one, and Job speaks to him directly as a person.
views.J: Rava read 10:7 as Job's attempt to 'free the whole world from judgment' by saying God created the righteous and the wicked (Bava Batra 16a). The rabbis drew on 10:10–11 in describing how a child is formed. Rashi reads 10:13 as Job saying that God had secretly intended his suffering all along.
views.X: Christian readers love 10:8–12 as a text for the dignity of every person from the womb, often cited with Psalm 139:13–16 and Jeremiah 1:5. Gregory the Great read Job's questions in 10:4–5 as pointing to the difference between God's eternal sight and ours. Many preachers treat 10:20–22 as an honest picture of the fear of death before the resurrection was revealed.

deep.h: Sheol, the land of no return
deep.b:
Job's last words in this chapter describe Sheol, the realm of the dead: 'the land of darkness and deep shadow', where there is 'no order' and even the light is gloom (10:21–22). The Hebrew Bible pictures Sheol as a place beneath the earth where all the dead go, righteous and wicked alike (3:17–19; Ecclesiastes 9:10). It is not described as a place of punishment, and those in it are cut off from God's praise (Psalm 6:5; Psalm 88:10–12).

Later Jewish and Christian belief came to distinguish the fates of the dead and to hope for resurrection (Daniel 12:2). The Greek and Latin translators of Job already show this development: the Vulgate's 'everlasting horror dwells there' (10:22) helped shape medieval pictures of hell. Job himself has no such hope yet. In chapter 14 he will imagine Sheol as a hiding place, and in 19:25–27 he will reach further.

echoes: 3:3–16; 7:7–21; 14:15; 33:6; Genesis 2:7; Genesis 3:19; Psalm 8:4; Psalm 119:73; Psalm 139:13–16; Psalm 138:8; Isaiah 64:8; Jeremiah 18:1–6; Jeremiah 20:14–18; Hosea 13:7–8; Ecclesiastes 11:5

settings.to: God, spoken aloud in the hearing of the three friends
settings.when: continuing his reply to Bildad, after wishing for someone to judge between him and God (9:33)
settings.why: to put his case directly to God: to ask for the charge, to remind God that he is his own handiwork, and to beg for a little relief before death. Since there is no one to stand between them, Job argues with God himself.
settings.readers: The first readers knew the lament psalms, which complain to God and appeal to his past care (Psalm 22; Psalm 44; Psalm 88). Job's prayer stretches that form to the limit, accusing God of a hidden plan. For a people asking where God's loyal love had gone after the exile (Lamentations 3; Psalm 89:49), it modeled a faith that speaks to God even when it cannot understand him.

title: Zophar: The Depths of God
sum: Zophar, the third friend, is the bluntest. Job's flood of words must not go unanswered; he mocks, and claims to be clean (11:2–4). Zophar wishes God would speak and show Job the secrets of wisdom: then Job would know that God is overlooking part of his guilt (11:5–6).

God's wisdom is higher than the heavens, deeper than Sheol, longer than the earth and wider than the sea; no one can search it out (11:7–9). God sees wickedness at once, and a fool will get sense when a wild donkey gives birth to a man (11:10–12). But if Job sets his heart right, prays, and puts away his sin, his life will be brighter than noon, he will rest secure, and many will seek his favor. The wicked, though, have only death to hope for (11:13–20).
readings: Read as a call to repentance

Zophar's second half (11:13–20) is a classic call to repentance, the language of the prophets and the psalms. His hymn to God's unsearchable wisdom (11:7–9) is echoed by Paul (Romans 11:33). Read alone, the chapter is good preaching.
Read as the hardest judgment

Zophar goes furthest of the friends. He calls Job a fool (11:12), accuses him of mocking (11:3), and says his suffering is less than he deserves (11:6). He uses God's mystery to end the conversation. Yet God's speeches, which also stress God's greater wisdom, do not condemn Job as Zophar does (42:7).

views.H: Traditional readers see Zophar as a real sage with sound doctrine wrongly applied. His praise of God's wisdom is true, but his assumption that Job is a hidden sinner is false. Some note that Zophar's wish that God would speak is answered in a way he did not expect.
views.C: Critical scholars point out that Zophar's appeal to God's hidden wisdom (11:6–9) anticipates themes of chapter 28 and the divine speeches (38–41). The poet gives the friends some of the best lines in the book, then judges them. Zophar has no speech in the third cycle, which many take as a sign that chapters 24–27 have been disturbed.
views.W: The theme of the gods' unsearchable will is common in Mesopotamian wisdom: 'Who knows the will of the gods in heaven?' asks the sufferer of Ludlul. The friend in the Babylonian Theodicy also says that the divine mind is as remote as the center of heaven. Zophar uses this commonplace not as a lament but as a rebuke.
views.J: Maimonides identifies Zophar with the view that everything happens by God's pure will, which no one may question (Guide 3.23). The rabbis treat Zophar as a sage who meant well. The Greek calls him king of the Minaeans, a people of Arabia.
views.X: Christian readers cherish 11:7–9 as a confession of God's incomprehensible greatness, quoted in sermons with Romans 11:33 and Ephesians 3:18. They also take Zophar as a warning: true doctrine about God's greatness can be used to silence the suffering. Gregory the Great read the friends as heretics who speak true things in a false spirit.

deep.h: Three friends, three kinds of certainty
deep.b:
By the end of the first round the reader has met three ways of being sure. Eliphaz rests on a night vision (4:12–21) and on experience (4:8). Bildad rests on the tradition of the fathers (8:8–10). Zophar rests on God's hidden wisdom, which he claims to know well enough to say what God would say (11:5–6). All three reach the same verdict: Job must have sinned, and he must repent.

Job's replies answer each in turn. He says that experience shows the wicked prospering (12:6; 21:7), that he knows the tradition as well as they do (12:3; 13:1–2), and that if God's wisdom is hidden, the friends cannot claim to speak for it (13:7–8). The book's ending supports Job's point: when God speaks, he does not repeat the friends' arguments (38–41), and he says they did not speak rightly about him (42:7).

settings.to: Job, with Eliphaz and Bildad present
settings.when: after Job's long reply to Bildad (9–10), which ended with Job begging God to leave him alone before he dies
settings.why: to rebuke Job's 'many words' and his claim to be clean, to insist that God's wisdom is beyond Job's knowing, and to call him to repent with a promise of restoration. Zophar aims to stop what he hears as blasphemy.
settings.readers: Readers, likely in Persian-era Judah, knew calls to repent and promises of restoration from the prophets (Isaiah 58; Zechariah 1:3). Zophar's speech shows how even those true promises can be used to accuse the suffering. It invites readers to ask whether they speak to the suffering as Zophar did.

title: Ask the Animals
sum: Job begins his longest reply with sarcasm: the friends must be the only wise people in the world (12:2). He knows as much as they do, yet he, who once called on God and was answered, has become a joke, while robbers live in peace (12:3–6).

Ask the animals, the birds, the earth and the fish: all of them know that 'the LORD's hand' has done this, the hand that holds every life (12:7–10). Then Job sings his own hymn of God's wisdom and power (12:13–25), and it is a hymn of overturning. God tears down and floods, strips counselors and judges, binds kings, leads priests away barefoot, silences elders, pours scorn on nobles, makes nations great and destroys them, and sends leaders stumbling in the dark like drunks.
readings: Read as sarcasm

Much of the chapter mocks the friends. Job parodies their claim to wisdom (12:2), their appeal to nature (12:7–10) and their hymns of God's power (12:13–25). His point is that he knows all this; what he does not see is justice.
Read as a theology of power

Job's hymn makes a serious claim: if God controls everything, he controls the collapse of nations and leaders too. The history of Israel's kings, priests and elders being led into exile (2 Kings 25) fits the hymn closely. For Job, God's wisdom is real, but it looks like power without moral order.

views.H: Traditional readers see Job defending himself against the friends' condescension while sharing their faith in God's sovereignty. Many note that Job's hymn is true: God does raise and bring down nations (Daniel 2:21). The question is only what it means for Job.
views.C: Critical scholars note the divine name YHWH in 12:9, the only use in the debate, and the near quotation of Isaiah 41:20 and Psalm 107:40. Some think 12:7–12 quotes the friends' lesson and 12:13–25 answers it. Many hear the exile in the hymn of overturned leaders.
views.W: Ancient hymns praise gods who raise and humble kings (for example, Babylonian hymns to Marduk). Job's hymn uses that form but leaves out any reason for the overturning. It is closer to the Egyptian 'Admonitions of Ipuwer', which describes a world turned upside down and asks where the god is.
views.J: Jewish commentators (Rashi, Ibn Ezra) discuss why the name YHWH appears in 12:9 and read 12:7–10 as Job's confession that God's providence reaches every creature. The rabbis read 12:12 as praising the wisdom of elders, though some note that Elihu disputes it (32:6–9).
views.X: Christian readers have taken 12:7–10 as an early form of the idea that creation reveals God (Romans 1:20) and 12:10 as a confession that every life is in God's hand. Mary's song, in which God 'brings down rulers' (Luke 1:52), echoes the same themes as 12:17–21, but with a reason: God lifts up the humble.

settings.what: Job's reply to Zophar, the longest speech of the first round
settings.to: Zophar and all three friends (12:1–13:19), then God (13:20–14:22)
settings.when: after Zophar's call to repentance, which ended the first round of speeches
settings.why: to answer all three friends at once: to reject their claim to superior wisdom, to show he knows God's power as well as they do, to accuse them of lying for God, and then to turn to God and argue his case directly. The speech moves from mockery to courtroom challenge to a meditation on death.
settings.readers: Readers after the exile, as the book's first readers likely were, could hear in Job's hymn of overturned kings, priests and elders (12:17–25) their own history, and in his challenge to the friends a warning against easy explanations of that history. The speech also teaches that one may know all the right doctrines and still have to wrestle with God.

title: Right to His Face
sum: Job tells the friends he knows all they know (13:1–2). He wants to argue with God, not with them; they are plasterers of lies and doctors who cure nothing, and their silence would be their wisdom (13:3–5). He accuses them of speaking falsely for God and of playing favorites in God's court; God himself will rebuke them for it (13:6–12).

Then Job resolves to speak, whatever it costs. He takes his life in his hands. In the famous line of 13:15 the written Hebrew says he has no hope, while the reading tradition (the KJV's 'Though he slay me, yet will I trust in him') says he will hope in God; both go on, 'but I will argue my ways to his face' (see the variant). Job has prepared his case and knows he is right (13:18). He turns to God, asks for two conditions, and demands to know his sins. Why does God hide his face and treat him as an enemy, a blown leaf, a prisoner in the stocks (13:20–28)?
readings: Read with the written text

Job expects death and argues anyway. His courage rests not on hope of survival but on integrity: he will not confess what he did not do. This is the reading the Plain follows (see the variant on 13:15).
Read with the reading tradition

Job's argument rests on trust: even at the cost of his life he will hope in God, and that hope is what lets him argue. The KJV made this the best-known line in Job, and Jewish and Christian tradition have cherished it.

views.H: Traditional readers usually follow the KJV and see 13:15 as the high point of Job's faith: he trusts God beyond death. They read Job's charge against the friends (13:7–10) as fulfilled in God's rebuke (42:7).
views.C: Many critical scholars prefer the written text of 13:15 as the harder reading, and read the chapter as Job's resolve to confront God in court at the risk of his life. They note how 13:7–10 anticipates 42:7–8.
views.W: No Mesopotamian sufferer challenges his god as Job does. The Babylonian Theodicy's sufferer complains, but submits; the sufferer of Ludlul praises Marduk for restoring him. Job's resolve to argue to God's face, at the risk of death, is without parallel in the wisdom of his neighbors.
views.J: The Mishnah uses 13:15 to debate whether Job served God out of love or out of fear, and concludes from 27:5 that it was love (Sotah 5:5). The Talmud (Sotah 31a) compares Job with Abraham on this point. Rashi follows the reading tradition: 'I will hope in him.'
views.X: Christian readers have made the KJV's 'Though he slay me, yet will I trust in him' a motto of faith under trial, from Gregory the Great through the Puritans to modern hymns. Paul's quotation of 13:16 in Philippians 1:19 shows the early church reading Job as a model for the suffering faithful.

deep.h: Why the Plain follows the written text at 13:15
deep.b: The variant on 13:15 gives the full case and the witnesses. In short: the written text is the harder reading, it fits the 'but' (akh) that opens the second line, and it matches Job's other words about lost hope (6:11; 14:19; 17:15; 19:10). The reading tradition is ancient (Mishnah Sotah 5:5), is followed by the Targum, the Vulgate and the KJV, and is also true to a man who keeps turning toward God. The reader can switch between them. What both share is the second line: whether from hope or from integrity, Job will not stop speaking to God.

In 13:7–12 Job makes a striking charge: the friends are telling lies on God's behalf, showing him favoritism the way a corrupt witness flatters a powerful party. They think they are defending God; Job says God does not want such defenders and will rebuke them (13:10). At the end of the book God does exactly that: 'You did not say what is right about me, the way my servant Job did' (42:7).

The passage has been used in many settings: against preachers who defend God with arguments they know to be weak, against religious leaders who protect institutions at the cost of the truth, and against comforters who explain suffering with easy answers. Its point is simple: God is honored by the truth, even an uncomfortable truth, not by flattery.

settings.when: after Job has told the friends to be silent and resolved to argue his case at the risk of his life (13:13–19)
settings.why: to set the conditions for a fair hearing (stop the pain and the terror), to demand to know his sins, and to plead the frailty of human life. Job wants God either to summon him or to answer him.
settings.readers: For readers who knew the lament psalms' cries ('How long will you hide your face?' Psalm 13:1), Job's prayer gave words to the experience of God's absence. It ends the first round of the debate in a meditation on death that speaks to every human being, not only to Israel.

title: A Tree Has Hope
sum: Job's prayer becomes a meditation on human life. A human born of a woman has few days and much turmoil; he blooms and withers like a flower, slips away like a shadow. Why should God bring such a creature to court? No one can make clean out of unclean. Since God has fixed the limits of human life, let him look away and let a man rest like a laborer at the end of the day (14:1–6).

A tree has hope: cut down, it sprouts again at the scent of water. But a man dies and is gone, and until the heavens are no more he will not wake (14:7–12). Job dares to wish that God would hide him in Sheol until his anger passes, then remember him; he would wait through his hard service until relief came, and God would long for the work of his hands (14:13–17). But the wish collapses: as water wears away stone, God wears away human hope. The dead man does not even know if his sons are honored; he feels only his own pain (14:18–22).
readings: Read as a lament for every human

Chapter 14 widens from Job's own case to the human condition. Its pictures, the flower, the shadow, the hired worker, the tree, the drying river, have made it a text for funerals for centuries. It speaks honestly about death without offering easy comfort.
Read as the first step of hope

Job does not believe in resurrection here; his answer to 14:14 seems to be no. But he imagines it, and the wish (14:13–17) is the first time anyone in the book reaches past death. Readers have seen this as the seed of the hope in 19:25–27, and later Jewish and Christian readers saw it as pointing to the resurrection.

views.H: Traditional Christian and Jewish readers have often read 14:14–15 as Job's faith that God will call him back from death, even if Job states it only as a hope. Others see Job speaking honestly from the limited knowledge of his time, before fuller revelation.
views.C: Critical scholars generally hold that Job expects no life after death, in line with most of the Hebrew Bible. The wish of 14:13–17 is a bold thought experiment, then rejected. Many date belief in resurrection in Israel to the later Persian or Hellenistic period (Isaiah 26:19; Daniel 12:2).
views.W: Mesopotamian texts describe the underworld as a 'land of no return', dark and dusty, where the dead eat clay (Descent of Ishtar; Gilgamesh, tablet 7). Gilgamesh's search for life ends with a plant of youth stolen by a snake. Job's picture of death is similar, but he imagines, for a moment, God himself calling the dead.
views.J: The rabbis cited 14:14 in discussions of the resurrection and noted that Job's 'no' was answered by later revelation (Isaiah 26:19; Daniel 12:2). Some rabbis said Job denied the resurrection, quoting 7:9 (Bava Batra 16a). Rashi reads 14:14 as 'if a man dies, will he live? No, so let me wait in life for my relief.'
views.X: Christian readers heard the 'change' of 14:14 (Vulgate immutatio) in Paul's 'we will all be changed' (1 Corinthians 15:51), and the tree of 14:7 in the shoot from Jesse's stump (Isaiah 11:1). The Book of Common Prayer burial service uses 14:1–2 at the graveside. Augustine and many others used the Greek of 14:4–5 for original sin.

deep.b:
Job sets two pictures side by side. A tree, even when cut down to the stump, even when its roots are old and dry, can sprout again 'at one whiff of water' (14:7–9). A man, by contrast, dies, lies limp, and is gone, like a lake that dries up and never fills again (14:10–12). The contrast is Job's whole point: nature renews, humans do not.

Yet the picture of the tree did not stay where Job put it. The prophets used the stump as the image of a future beyond judgment: 'a shoot will come out from the stump of Jesse' (Isaiah 11:1), 'the holy seed is its stump' (Isaiah 6:13). Job's own word for the tree's new growth, yachalif, shares a root with the 'relief' he longs for in 14:14, chalifati. The very image he uses to deny human hope carries a seed of it. Later in the book Job says God 'rips my hope up by the roots like a tree' (19:10), but in the same speech he says, 'I know that my redeemer lives' (19:25).

deep.title: Claude's theory: 14:13–15 answers 10:8–12
deep.b: The wish of 14:13–15 seems built to answer chapter 10. There Job said God's hands made him (10:8–12), but that God would reject the work of his hands (10:3), and asked to be left alone before he went to the land of darkness (10:20–22). Here he imagines God hiding him in that very darkness, not to forget him but to 'remember' him, and longing for 'the thing your hands had made' (14:15). The same three elements, God's handiwork, Sheol and God's attention, are rearranged from a nightmare into a hope. If this is right, chapters 10 and 14 frame Job's two speeches of the first round as one argument with God that moves, briefly, from fear toward hope. Commentators note the link between 10:3 and 14:15 (Clines); the larger pattern is my suggestion.

traditions.q: Does every human inherit the guilt of Adam's sin, or only its effects?
views: Catholic

Original sin is passed on 'by propagation, not by imitation': every child inherits a fallen nature deprived of original holiness, a sin 'contracted, not committed', which baptism takes away (Council of Trent, Session 5; Catechism 404–405).
Orthodox

Humans inherit the consequences of Adam's sin, above all mortality and a weakened nature, but not Adam's personal guilt; each person is guilty only of the sins they commit. Many Orthodox teachers speak of 'ancestral sin' rather than inherited guilt.
Lutheran

Since the fall all people are born with sin, 'without the fear of God, without trust in God, and with concupiscence', and this disease 'is truly sin, condemning' those not born again (Augsburg Confession 2).
Reformed
The guilt of Adam's first sin is imputed to all his descendants, and a corrupted nature is passed on by ordinary generation (Westminster Confession 6.3, which cites Job 14:4 among its proof texts).
Methodist
Original sin is the corruption of every person's nature, inclining to evil (Articles of Religion 7); John Wesley taught it strongly, while also teaching prevenient grace given to all.

traditions.q: Are the dead conscious before the resurrection, or do they 'sleep' until then (14:12)?
views: Catholic
At death each soul faces a particular judgment and enters heaven, purification (purgatory) or hell at once, awaiting the resurrection of the body (Catechism 1021–1022, 1030).
Orthodox
The souls of the dead are conscious and experience a foretaste of their final state; the church prays for the departed and asks the saints' prayers, awaiting the general resurrection.
Reformed
The souls of the righteous are received at once into heaven, and those of the wicked into hell, while their bodies rest until the resurrection (Westminster Confession 32.1).
Adventist
Death is an unconscious state, a sleep, until the resurrection at Christ's return; texts such as Job 14:12 and Ecclesiastes 9:5 are read literally (Seventh-day Adventist Fundamental Beliefs 26).
Jehovah's Witnesses
The dead have no conscious existence; the hope is a resurrection in which God recreates the person, and Job 14:13–15 is read as Job's hope for that.
